svg.title: The 32-bit MPLS label: field widths, what each field is for, and the two reserved labels that appear in every design
svg.desc: A bit ruler from bit 0 to bit 31 split into the four fields: a 20-bit label value, a 3-bit EXP field now called traffic class, a 1-bit bottom-of-stack flag and an 8-bit TTL. Each field carries a note on why a designer cares: the label range and the reserved 0 to 15, EXP mapping DSCP to the MPLS traffic class, the S bit telling the egress PE this is the last label, and TTL being copied from the IP header so traceroute and loop detection still work. Two reserved labels are drawn with their behaviour: label 3, implicit null, where the penultimate hop pops and the egress receives plain IP, and label 0, IPv4 explicit null, where the penultimate hop swaps to 0 so the egress PE still sees the EXP bits. A closing panel gives the design rule about end-to-end QoS depending on which of the two is used.
svg.text: Four bytes, four fields — and two of them decide whether your QoS survives to the last hop
Memorise the widths once; most MPLS arguments in a design review come down to the 3-bit field
source of the two labels below.
QoS class carried with the label.
same granularity as an IP header.
Bottom of stack. When it is 1,
this is the last label: after
Copied from the IP TTL. Keeps
THE TWO RESERVED LABELS YOU WILL MEET EVERY WEEK
The penultimate hop pops the label and sends plain IP.
Egress PE does one lookup instead of two: cheaper and faster.
But the EXP bits are gone. The egress PE cannot queue on
MPLS class for the last segment, only on the IP header.
Label 0 · IPv4 explicit null · PHP disabled
The penultimate hop swaps to label 0 instead of popping.
The egress PE still sees a label, so it still sees EXP.
Costs one extra label operation and one extra lookup; buys
end-to-end QoS enforcement at the egress, plus a visible
Design rule: if the service needs end-to-end QoS for voice or video across the MPLS core, ask the carrier which of these two is in use on the last hop.
“Voice is degraded inside the carrier network” is almost always PHP discarding EXP, not a bandwidth shortage. Put the answer in the design document, with the carrier's name next to it.
